title: Copying: Assignment, Shallow Copy, and Deep Copy
description: The difference between assignment, shallow copies, and deep copies, especially for nested mutable structures.
objectives: Understand what a shallow copy does and doesn't copy
Use copy.deepcopy() for fully independent nested structures

content.heading: Assignment vs. Shallow Copy
content.body:
b = a never copies a mutable object — it makes b an alias, another name for the exact same object as a. Any mutation through either name is visible through the other. To actually get a new, independent object, you need an explicit copy. list(a), a.copy(), or a[:] all create a shallow copy: a new outer container, but populated with references to the same inner elements as the original. For a flat list of immutable values (numbers, strings), a shallow copy behaves exactly like an independent copy, since those inner elements can't be mutated in place anyway.

The distinction becomes critical for nested mutable structures: a shallow copy of a list of lists creates a new outer list, but the inner lists inside it are still the very same objects as in the original — mutating an inner list through the copy still affects the original.

content.heading: Deep Copy and the copy Module
content.body: The copy module's copy.copy(obj) explicitly performs a shallow copy (same behavior as the shortcuts above but works generically on any type, not just lists). copy.deepcopy(obj) recursively copies every nested object it finds, producing a result with no shared mutable state with the original at any level — the only way to guarantee a truly independent nested structure. Deep copying costs more time and memory proportional to the structure's total size, so it should be used deliberately, not by default, when a shallow copy would suffice.

content.code:
import copy

original = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
shallow = copy.copy(original)
shallow[0][0] = 99
print(original[0][0])          # 99 — inner list was shared!

deep = copy.deepcopy(original)
deep[0][0] = -1
print(original[0][0])          # still 99 — deep copy is fully independent
content.explanation: The shallow copy's outer list is new, but its inner lists are shared with original, so mutating shallow[0] leaks into original. deepcopy() recursively duplicates every nested list, fully isolating the two structures.

keyPoints: b = a aliases the same object — it is not a copy at all
A shallow copy (list(a), a.copy(), a[:], copy.copy()) copies the outer container only
Nested mutable objects are still shared between the original and a shallow copy
copy.deepcopy() recursively copies everything, at the cost of more time/memory
commonMistakes: Assuming a.copy() fully isolates a list of lists (it doesn't — only the outer list is new)
Confusing plain assignment with copying entirely
Reaching for deepcopy() by default even when a shallow copy (or no copy at all) would be sufficient and faster
